planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Arnold's Pride grows noticeably faster than typical seedling Chinese fringetree and forms a strong central leader with minimal training.

directions: Selected at the Arnold Arboretum from a seedling noted for unusually vigorous, upright growth and a well-formed central leader, this cultivar carries the species' frothy spring display of slender white flower clusters on a faster-maturing, more tree-like frame than most seed-grown Chinese fringetrees. Unlike the typically dioecious species, Arnold's Pride sets fruit on its own, producing clusters of dark blue-black, olive-like fruit each fall that draw songbirds without needing a separate pollinator tree nearby. Plant in average, medium-moisture, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade for the heaviest bloom, and expect handsome exfoliating gray-brown bark to become a strong winter feature as the tree matures into a 25-foot specimen. It tolerates urban conditions well and needs little pruning beyond removing crossing branches while young.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Spirit's compact, weeping habit makes it well suited to small urban lots and planting strips where a full-sized fringetree would not fit.

directions: Originating at Norfolk Botanical Garden, Spirit is a distinctly compact, weeping selection of Chinese fringetree that reaches only a fraction of the species' typical size in its first decade while still smothering its cascading branches in fragrant, slender white flower clusters each late spring. The pendulous habit and uniform, predictable crown form make it a reliable choice for street tree plantings and small residential gardens where straight seedling trees would be too variable in shape and ultimate size. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to filtered light, and stake young trees loosely if needed to establish a strong leader before the weeping habit fully develops. It shares the species' good heat and urban tolerance and needs only light structural pruning once established.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
